Part I · Lectures 21 and 22

Lecture primer

Object detection answers two questions at once: what is in the image, and where. Each answer is a set of labelled boxes with confidence scores.

Two-stage detectors
Propose regions, then classify each one: R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN (A3–A6).
Single-pass detectors
Predict boxes and classes for the whole image in one network pass: YOLO, DETR (A7–A8). SSD and CenterNet in the notebook belong here too.
Evaluation
Remove duplicates with NMS, match predictions to ground truth by IoU, then summarise with AP and mAP (A9–A11).

Further viewing. Justin Johnson's recorded lectures cover the same material with more architecture detail: Lecture 15, Object Detection,1 and Lecture 16, Detection and Segmentation.2 Several diagrams below are redrawn from Lecture 15.

A1 · Lecture 21, slides 6–12 and 17

Detection as classification of image windows

Classification asks "is this a giraffe?". Detection asks "where is the giraffe?", and the standard answer is to ask the classification question for every window of the image.

A sliding window has three free parameters: its stride, its scale and its shape (aspect ratio). Objects come in unknown sizes, so a range of scales and shapes is needed, and the number of windows multiplies:

$$N_{\text{windows}} = N_{\text{positions}} \times N_{\text{scales}} \times N_{\text{shapes}}.$$
IllustrativeSliding windows over a COCO image

Halving the stride quadruples the number of positions. Every extra window is one more classification, and one more chance of a false alarm (slide 15).

A2 · Lecture 21, slides 13–14

Intersection over union

A detection is judged by how well its box overlaps the true box. Intersection over union (IoU) divides the shared area by the area covered by either box:

$$\operatorname{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B| - |A \cap B|}.$$

It is 1 for identical boxes and 0 for disjoint ones. A detection counts as correct when its IoU with a true box reaches a threshold, usually 0.5.

LiveDrag either box, or its lower-right corner to resize it
ground truth \(A\)prediction \(B\)
Quick check · IoU on a grid

The ground truth covers cells \(x \in [0, 4]\), \(y \in [0, 4]\) (a \(4 \times 4\) square). A prediction covers \(x \in [2, 6]\), \(y \in [0, 4]\).

IoU of the two boxes:
Show solution

The boxes share a \(2 \times 4\) strip, so \(|A \cap B| = 8\) and \(|A \cup B| = 16 + 16 - 8 = 24\), giving \(\operatorname{IoU} = 8/24 = 1/3\). Shifting a box by half its width already drops it below 0.5.

A3 · Lecture 21, slides 18–32

Region proposals and R-CNN

Instead of every window, R-CNN classifies about 2000 regions of interest (RoIs) that are likely to contain objects. Selective Search proposes them by over-segmenting the image into superpixels and repeatedly merging adjacent ones by colour, texture, size and compactness.3

Each RoI is warped to \(224 \times 224\), run through a CNN, and given a class label and a box correction.4 The classifier has \(N + 1\) outputs: the \(N\) object classes and "background".

IllustrativeFour detector architectures built from the same blocks
runs once per imageruns once per region (drawn as a stack)where the regions come from
Advantage (slide 32)
Far fewer classifications than an exhaustive sliding window.
Disadvantages
Still about 2000 CNN passes per image, and an object missed by Selective Search can never be detected.
A4 · Lecture 21, slides 26–27

Bounding-box regression

A proposal is rarely exactly on the object. The network therefore predicts a transform \((t_x, t_y, t_w, t_h)\) that corrects the proposal \(p = (p_x, p_y, p_w, p_h)\), where \((p_x, p_y)\) is its centre.

Step 1 translates the centre by a fraction of the box size:

$$b_x = p_x + p_w\,t_x, \qquad b_y = p_y + p_h\,t_y.$$

Step 2 rescales the width and height:

$$b_w = p_w\,e^{t_w}, \qquad b_h = p_h\,e^{t_h}.$$
LiveProposal, transform and corrected box
proposal \(p\)corrected box \(b\)ground truth
Derivation · why the size uses an exponential

A width must stay positive, and a correction should mean the same for a large and a small box. Predicting \(t_w = \ln(b_w / p_w)\) gives both: any real \(t_w\) maps to a positive \(b_w\), and doubling the box is \(t_w = \ln 2\) whatever its size.

The training targets are therefore

$$t_x = \frac{g_x - p_x}{p_w}, \quad t_y = \frac{g_y - p_y}{p_h}, \quad t_w = \ln\frac{g_w}{p_w}, \quad t_h = \ln\frac{g_h}{p_h},$$

for a ground-truth box \(g\). "Set the regression targets" above fills them in.

A5 · Lecture 21, slides 33–48

Fast R-CNN and RoI pooling

Fast R-CNN runs the whole image through a fully convolutional backbone once, then crops each RoI from the last feature map.5 To give every RoI the same size, RoI pooling snaps the box to feature-map cells, divides it into a fixed grid, and max-pools within each grid cell.

With a \(640 \times 480\) image and a \(20 \times 15\) feature map, one feature column covers \(32 \times 32\) pixels:

$$\text{stride} = \frac{640}{20} = \frac{480}{15} = 32.$$
IllustrativeDrag the box: it snaps to feature cells and is pooled to a \(2 \times 2\) grid (slides 39–40)
\(20 \times 15\) feature map over a \(640 \times 480\) image
pooled \(2 \times 2\) output (one channel)
Top: the same box followed through the pipeline (adapted from J. Johnson, Lecture 15).1

Training uses a multi-task loss: cross-entropy for the class plus a smooth \(\ell_1\) loss on the box parameters, counted only for object classes (slide 47):

$$L = L_{\text{cls}} + L_{\text{loc}}, \qquad \operatorname{smooth}_{\ell_1}(e) = \begin{cases} 0.5\,e^2 & |e| < 1 \\ |e| - 0.5 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
IllustrativeSmooth \(\ell_1\) against the squared and absolute errors
\(\operatorname{smooth}_{\ell_1}(e)\)\(0.5\,e^2\)\(|e|\)
Quadratic near zero, so small errors give gentle gradients; linear far away, so an outlier box cannot dominate the loss.

Fast R-CNN is about 9 times faster to train and 140 times faster at test time than R-CNN (slide 48), but its RoIs still come from Selective Search.

IllustrativeWhere the backbone ends and the per-region network begins (slides 44–46)
The backbone runs once on the whole image; the layers after RoI pooling run once per region, so they are kept light. With AlexNet the five conv layers form the backbone and the two FC layers the per-region network; with ResNet-50 the last stage runs per region. Adapted from J. Johnson, Lecture 15 (2019).1
A6 · Lecture 21, slides 49–54

Faster R-CNN and anchor boxes

Faster R-CNN learns the proposals too.6 A region proposal network (RPN) places an anchor point at every feature-map column, and each anchor point carries \(k\) boxes of fixed sizes and aspect ratios.

For each anchor box the RPN predicts an objectness score (object or background) and a box transform, exactly as in A4. The best proposals then go through the Fast R-CNN head.

$$N_{\text{anchors}} = W_{\text{feat}} \times H_{\text{feat}} \times k.$$
IllustrativeClick a feature-map column to see its anchor boxes

The RPN and the detection head share one backbone, so proposals cost almost nothing: Faster R-CNN tests about 10 times faster than Fast R-CNN (slide 54).

A7 · Lecture 22, slides 13–17

YOLO: one network pass, one output tensor

YOLO v1 skips proposals.7 It divides the image into an \(S \times S\) grid. Each cell predicts \(B\) boxes, each with five numbers \((x, y, w, h, \text{confidence})\), and one set of \(C\) class probabilities.

The whole output is a single tensor:

$$S \times S \times (5B + C) = 7 \times 7 \times (5 \cdot 2 + 20) = 7 \times 7 \times 30 .$$

The cell that contains an object's centre is responsible for detecting it.

IllustrativeThe grid cell responsible for each object
Loss (slide 16)
Sum-squared error between predicted and true maps; box coordinates weighted up, empty cells excluded from the class loss.
Limitation (slide 23)
One cell predicts only \(B\) boxes, so small objects packed together are hard; it is faster but less accurate than two-stage detectors.
A8 · Lecture 22, slides 18–23

DETR: detection as set prediction

DETR treats the output as a set of \(N\) (label, box) pairs, usually \(N = 100\).8 A CNN backbone and a transformer encoder produce image tokens. A transformer decoder turns \(N\) learned "object queries" into \(N\) predictions; queries without an object predict "no object".

Training first finds the one-to-one assignment \(\hat\sigma\) between ground truth and predictions with the lowest total matching cost, then applies the loss to those pairs:

$$\hat\sigma = \arg\min_{\sigma}\ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{C}\big(y_i,\ \hat y_{\sigma(i)}\big).$$
IllustrativeBipartite matching on slide 21's example
Cost of a pair: \(1\) if the classes differ, plus the \(\ell_1\) box distance divided by 1000. Unmatched "no object" pairs cost 0. Click a ground-truth row, then a prediction, to make your own assignment.

Because each object is matched to exactly one prediction, DETR does not produce duplicate detections and needs no NMS (slide 23).

A9 · Lecture 22, slides 25–30

Non-maximum suppression

Detectors return many overlapping boxes for the same object. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) keeps one:

  1. Take the highest-scoring remaining box and keep it.
  2. Drop every lower-scoring box that overlaps it with IoU above a threshold, for example 0.7.
  3. Repeat with the next highest-scoring box. Usually done separately for each class.
IllustrativeNMS step by step on two zebras

A low threshold also suppresses correct boxes on objects that overlap each other (slide 30); a high threshold keeps duplicates.

A10 · Lecture 22, slides 31–41

Precision, recall and average precision

For one class, sort all detections by score. Walk down the list: a detection that matches an unused ground-truth box with IoU \(\ge 0.5\) is a true positive and uses up that box; otherwise it is a false positive. After each detection:

$$\text{precision} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}, \qquad \text{recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{number of ground-truth boxes}}.$$

Average precision (AP) is the area under the resulting precision–recall curve.

IllustrativeThe dog example of slides 32–41: click a detection to switch it between TP and FP
recall · precision

The slide reports dog AP \(\approx 0.86\): joining the points with straight lines gives 0.850, the interpolated rule below gives 0.865. The exact number depends on how the gaps between points are filled. COCO, and FiftyOne in the notebook, replace each precision by the best precision at any higher recall, then average it at 101 recall levels \(0, 0.01, \dots, 1\).9

Quick check · the best possible AP (slide 40)
Five detections, three ground-truth dogs. What is the largest AP any ordering can achieve?
Show solution

If the three true positives have the three highest scores, precision is 1 at recall \(1/3, 2/3, 1\), and AP = 1. The false positives come after recall 1, so they cost nothing. AP rewards ranking correct detections above wrong ones.

A11 · Lecture 22, slides 41–43

Mean average precision and COCO mAP

The mean average precision (mAP) averages AP over classes. The lecture's example (slide 42):

$$\text{mAP}@0.5 = \frac{0.65 + 0.80 + 0.86}{3} = 0.77 .$$

COCO mAP also averages over ten IoU thresholds, \(0.50, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\), so it rewards boxes that are tight, not just roughly right:

$$\text{COCO mAP} = \frac{1}{10} \sum_{t \in \{0.50, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\}} \text{mAP}@t .$$
LivemAP of the notebook's detector at each IoU threshold (25 images)
IoU threshold \(t\) · \(\text{mAP}@t\); the dashed line is their mean, the COCO mAP

One number hides a lot (slide 43): classification errors, loose boxes, misses and false alarms all lower mAP. The rest of this page looks inside it.

Part II · worksheet12_colab_new.ipynb

Notebook walkthrough

The notebook downloads a pre-trained detector from the TensorFlow 2 Model Zoo,10 runs it on 25 of the workshop's 50 COCO 2017 validation images, and evaluates the detections with FiftyOne.11

We ran the same code on a CPU with TensorFlow 2.21 and stored every detection with score at least 0.05. Every chart below is computed in your browser from those detections, with FiftyOne's matching and AP rules. The code cells are collapsed; their numbers follow the notebook.

Notebook section 2(1)–(2) · cells 9–12

The model zoo: speed against accuracy

The Model Zoo's detectors were all trained on COCO 2017, with its 80 object classes.9 Their names give the architecture, the backbone and the input size, for example ssd_mobilenet_v1_fpn_640x640.

The notebook uses SSD MobileNet V1 FPN 640×640: a single-pass SSD head12 on a MobileNet backbone13 with a feature pyramid.14

Model Zoo tableSpeed and COCO mAP of the ten suggested models (cell 9)
Faster R-CNN (two-stage)SSDCenterNetthe notebook's model
time per image (ms, lower is faster) · COCO mAP (higher is better)

    No model is both fastest and most accurate. The two most accurate, CenterNet Hourglass-104 (41.9) and Faster R-CNN Inception-ResNet V2 (37.7), use the heaviest backbones and are among the slowest: the speed–accuracy trade-off of lecture 21, slide 54.15

    Cell 10Download and extract a model from the zoo · show code
    Cell 10Download and extract a model from the zoo
    # Download and extract model
def download_model(model_name, model_date):
    base_url = 'http://download.tensorflow.org/models/object_detection/tf2/'
    model_file = model_name + '.tar.gz'
    model_dir = tf.keras.utils.get_file(fname=model_name,
                                        origin=base_url + model_date + '/' + model_file,
                                        untar=True, #Whether the file should be decompressed
                                        cache_dir="../../") #Location to store cached files

    model_dir = os.path.join(model_dir, model_name)
    return str(model_dir)
MODEL_DATE = '20200711'
MODEL_NAME = 'ssd_mobilenet_v1_fpn_640x640_coco17_tpu-8'
PATH_TO_MODEL_DIR = download_model(MODEL_NAME, MODEL_DATE)

    Making predictions

    Cell 30 runs the detector on 25 images. The model returns up to 100 boxes per image, each as \([y_{\min}, x_{\min}, y_{\max}, x_{\max}]\) relative to the image, with a COCO class id and a score.

    The loop keeps boxes with score at least min_score_thresh = 0.3 and converts each one to FiftyOne's convention:

    $$[x, y, w, h] = [x_{\min},\ y_{\min},\ x_{\max} - x_{\min},\ y_{\max} - y_{\min}] .$$

    Cell 30Run the detector and store the predictions · show code
    Cell 30Run the detector and store the predictions
    def load_image_into_numpy_array(path):
    """Load an image from file into a numpy array.

    Puts image into numpy array to feed into tensorflow graph.
    Note that by convention we put it into a numpy array with shape
    (height, width, channels), where channels=3 for RGB.

    Args:
      path: the file path to the image

    Returns:
      uint8 numpy array with shape (img_height, img_width, 3)
    """
    return np.array(Image.open(path).convert("RGB"))

# Exercise 3: set to True to test the detector on grayscale copies of the images
GRAYSCALE = False

# Choose a random subset of 25 samples to add predictions.
# The larger the sample you choose, the longer it will take.
predictions_view = coco_dataset.take(25, seed=51)

# Get class list
ids_to_index = {cat["id"]: idx for idx, cat in enumerate(coco_dataset.info["categories"])}
classes = [cat["name"] for cat in coco_dataset.info["categories"]]
print(len(classes))
print(classes)

# Add predictions to samples
with fo.ProgressBar() as pb:
    for sample in pb(predictions_view):

        # Load image
        image_np = load_image_into_numpy_array(sample.filepath)
        if GRAYSCALE:  # keep three channels, drop the colour
            image_np = np.stack([np.array(Image.fromarray(image_np).convert("L"))] * 3, axis=-1)

        # Convert image to tensor
        input_tensor = tf.convert_to_tensor(image_np)
        input_tensor = input_tensor[tf.newaxis, ...]  # Add batch dimension

        # Run detection
        detections = detect_fn(input_tensor)

        # Process detections
        num_detections = int(detections.pop("num_detections"))
        detections = {
            key: value[0, :num_detections].numpy()
            for key, value in detections.items()
        }
        detections["num_detections"] = num_detections

        # Convert classes to ints
        detections["detection_classes"] = detections["detection_classes"].astype(np.int64)

        result_detections = []

        for label, score, box in zip(
            detections["detection_classes"],
            detections["detection_scores"],
            detections["detection_boxes"]
        ):
            if score < min_score_thresh:
                continue

            ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax = box
            rel_box = [xmin, ymin, xmax - xmin, ymax - ymin]

            result_detections.append(
                fo.Detection(
                    label=classes[ids_to_index[label]],
                    bounding_box=rel_box,
                    confidence=float(score),
                )
            )

        # Save predictions to dataset

        sample["mytest"] = fo.Detections(detections=result_detections)
        sample.save()

    Metric definitions

    True positive (TP)
    A prediction matched to an unused ground-truth box of the same class with IoU \(\ge\) the threshold.
    False positive (FP)
    A prediction with no such match: wrong place, wrong class, or a duplicate.
    False negative (FN)
    A ground-truth box that no prediction matched. True negatives are not counted: every empty window would be one.

    Precision, recall and their harmonic mean \(F_1\):

    $$P = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}, \qquad R = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R} .$$

    Averaging over classes can be done three ways. The micro average pools the counts of all classes first; the macro average gives every class equal weight; the weighted average weights each class by its number of ground-truth objects (its support \(n_c\)):

    $$P_{\text{micro}} = \frac{\sum_c \text{TP}_c}{\sum_c (\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c)}, \qquad P_{\text{macro}} = \frac{1}{|C|}\sum_c P_c, \qquad P_{\text{weighted}} = \frac{\sum_c n_c P_c}{\sum_c n_c} .$$
    Quick check · micro versus macro

    Class "person": 16 TP, 17 FP. Class "car": 0 TP, 2 FP.

    1. Micro-averaged precision:
    2. Macro-averaged precision:
    Show solution

    Micro: \(16 / 35 \approx 0.457\). Macro: \((16/33 + 0)/2 \approx 0.242\). One rare class with no hits halves the macro average but barely moves the micro average.

    Notebook section 3(2) · cells 34–35

    Running the evaluation

    evaluate_detections matches predictions to ground truth class by class. Within each image and class it takes predictions from the highest score down, and gives each one the unused ground-truth box with the largest IoU, if that IoU reaches iou=0.5.

    With compute_mAP=True it also repeats the matching at the ten COCO thresholds, \(0.50, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\). So the printed mAP is the COCO mAP of A11; iou=0.5 only sets the per-object TP/FP labels.

    Cell 35Evaluate the predictions · show code
    Cell 35Evaluate the predictions
    # Evaluate the predictions in the model field of our `predictions_view`
# with respect to the objects in the `ground_truth_detections` field

results = predictions_view.evaluate_detections(
    pred_field = "mytest", #the name of the field containing the predicted
    gt_field="ground_truth_detections", #the name of the field containing the ground truth
    compute_mAP=True,
    iou=0.5, #the IoU threshold to use to determine matches
    eval_key="eval", #store per-sample and per-object results under "eval"
)

print("\nmAP: %.4f" % results.mAP())

    Exercises

    Exercises 1–3 ask you to change the notebook and observe. The detections for those changes were run offline with the same code, so you can explore them here. Exercise 4 is a calculation by hand.

    Exercise 1 · Lecture 21, slides 44–54 · Lecture 22, slides 13–23

    Comparing detector architectures and backbones

    Problem statement

    Compare and contrast the results of Faster R-CNN, SSD and CenterNet. Also try swapping the backbone of a network (for example ResNet against MobileNet) to see if it changes the results.

    Prerequisite 1.1 · Three detector families
    Faster R-CNN
    Two stages: an RPN proposes regions from anchors, then a second head classifies and refines each one (A6).
    SSD (RetinaNet when it uses ResNet + FPN)
    One stage: anchors at several feature-map scales are classified and regressed directly, with no second look.1216
    CenterNet
    One stage, no anchors: a heatmap per class whose peaks are object centres, plus a predicted width and height at each peak.17 It extends YOLO's "heatmap per class" idea (A7).

    For a longer comparison of two-stage and single-stage detectors, see Johnson's Lectures 15 and 16.12

    Prerequisite 1.2 · The backbone

    The backbone is the feature extractor shared by every head (lecture 21, slides 44–46). MobileNet replaces full convolutions by depthwise-separable ones, which cuts computation roughly eight-fold; ResNet-50 is deeper and more accurate.1318 Swapping it while keeping the detector head isolates the backbone's effect. A5 shows where the backbone ends.

    Warm-up exercise · reading the Model Zoo table

    From cell 9: SSD MobileNet V1 FPN takes 48 ms at 29.1 mAP; SSD ResNet50 V1 FPN takes 46 ms at 34.3 mAP; Faster R-CNN Inception ResNet V2 takes 206 ms at 37.7 mAP.

    1. How many mAP points does the ResNet-50 backbone add to SSD?
    2. How many times slower is the most accurate Faster R-CNN than SSD ResNet50?
    Show solution

    ResNet-50 adds 5.2 mAP points to SSD at no measured speed cost on the zoo's TPU; on our CPU it takes 0.60 s per image against 0.54 s. The best two-stage model adds another 3.4 points for 4.5 times the time.

    Bridge to the question. The zoo's numbers are averages over 5000 images. Below, the four models run on the same 25 workshop images, so you can see where they differ object by object.

    Which model finds the most objects? Which is most precise? Does the backbone or the architecture matter more?
    PrecomputedFour detectors on the 25 evaluated images (min_score_thresh = 0.3)
    PrecomputedThe same image through each detector
    LiveAP at IoU 0.5 by class, for each detector
    Answer to Exercise 1
    • Backbone first. Swapping MobileNet for ResNet-50 under the same SSD head raises COCO mAP on the 25 images from 0.450 to 0.521 and recall from 0.65 to 0.74, for about 1.1 times the CPU time. The zoo shows the same gap (29.1 against 34.3).
    • Architecture alone does not decide. With a ResNet-50 backbone at 640×640, Faster R-CNN scores below SSD here (0.423) and on the zoo table (29.3 against 34.3). Its second look pays off with stronger backbones and larger inputs: the Inception-ResNet version reaches 37.7.
    • Different error profiles. Faster R-CNN and CenterNet keep fewer boxes above 0.3 (145 and 133 against about 200 for SSD), so they are more precise (0.54 and 0.56) but find fewer objects. SSD ResNet-50 has the best recall and the tightest boxes (mAP@0.75 of 0.573).
    • CenterNet is the fastest on our CPU (0.24 s per image): no anchors, no RoI stage, a smaller 512×512 input.
    • With 25 images the ranking is noisy: many classes have one or two objects, so a single detection swings a class's AP between 0 and 1. Conclusions need the full validation set.
    Exercise 2 · Lecture 21, slides 12 and 29 · Lecture 22, slides 31–41

    The effect of the score threshold

    Problem statement

    Try changing min_score_thresh in 2(4) Make predictions to other values between 0 and 1. How does this affect the results of detections? Why?

    Prerequisite 2.1 · A threshold picks one point on the P–R curve

    Sorting detections by score and sweeping a threshold traces the precision–recall curve (A10). A fixed threshold keeps only detections above it: it picks one operating point on that curve.

    Raising it removes low-confidence detections. Those are more often false positives, so precision tends to rise, while recall can only fall:

    $$\tau_1 < \tau_2 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{TP}(\tau_2) \le \text{TP}(\tau_1) \ \Longrightarrow\ R(\tau_2) \le R(\tau_1) .$$
    Warm-up exercise · one class, two thresholds

    Six detections, sorted by score, with 4 ground-truth objects: scores \(0.95, 0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.35, 0.2\); outcomes TP, TP, FP, TP, FP, TP.

    1. Threshold 0.6: precision and recall
    2. Threshold 0.1: precision and recall
    Show solution

    At 0.6: \(P = 2/3\), \(R = 2/4 = 0.5\). At 0.1: \(P = 4/6 = 2/3\), \(R = 4/4 = 1\). Lowering the threshold doubled recall here at no loss of precision; in general it trades precision for recall.

    Bridge to the question. The same sweep on the real detections shows precision, recall and mAP move in different ways, and why.

    Move the threshold. Why does mAP fall as the threshold rises, even when precision improves?
    LivePrecision, recall, \(F_1\) and mAP against min_score_thresh (SSD MobileNet, 25 images)
    precision (micro, IoU 0.5)recall\(F_1\)COCO mAP
    The image viewer in 2(4) uses the same threshold control; set it there to see which boxes appear and disappear.
    Answer to Exercise 2
    • Higher threshold: fewer detections. Uncertain boxes, which are mostly false positives, go first, so precision rises; but some true objects are dropped too, so recall falls.
    • Lower threshold: more detections, higher recall, more false alarms and lower precision.
    • Why mAP falls as the threshold rises: AP is the area under the whole P–R curve, traced by sweeping a threshold over the scores. Applying min_score_thresh first cuts that curve off at the recall it reaches; the missing part contributes nothing. Lowering the threshold can only add points at higher recall, so mAP never decreases as the threshold falls.
    • Choosing a value depends on the application: a high threshold when false alarms are expensive, a low one when misses are. For computing mAP, keep a low threshold and let AP do the sweep.
    Exercise 3 · Lecture 21, slides 28 and 55

    Robustness to modified input images

    Problem statement

    Modify some of the input images and see if detection still works, for example by converting the images to grayscale (set GRAYSCALE = True in 2(4) Make predictions), or by splitting your own sub-dataset from COCO (2(3), optional).

    Prerequisite 3.1 · Distribution shift

    The detectors were trained on COCO's colour photos. A modified input is a test image from a different distribution: features the network learnt to rely on, such as the orange of a carrot, may be missing.

    To keep the network's input shape, a grayscale image is copied into all three channels:

    $$Y = 0.299\,R + 0.587\,G + 0.114\,B, \qquad (R', G', B') = (Y, Y, Y).$$
    Warm-up exercise · what grayscale removes
    1. A carrot-orange pixel \((255, 128, 0)\) becomes which gray level?
    2. A green pixel \((0, 255, 0)\) becomes which gray level?
    Show solution

    Orange becomes 151 and green 150. Orange and green, easy to tell apart in colour, are identical in grayscale: carrots next to broccoli lose their colour cue and must be recognised by shape and texture alone.

    Bridge to the question. Below, the four detectors see grayscale versions of the same 25 images, and the notebook's model also sees blurred ones.

    Which classes suffer most without colour? Does blur hurt more than grayscale?
    PrecomputedCOCO mAP on original and modified images (25 images)
    originalgrayscaleGaussian blur, \(\sigma = 3\) px (SSD MobileNet only)
    PrecomputedOne image, three inputs (SSD MobileNet)
    LiveChange in AP at IoU 0.5 per class, grayscale minus original (SSD MobileNet)
    Answer to Exercise 3
    • Detection still works on grayscale images, with a modest drop: COCO mAP falls by 3% (CenterNet) to 14% (SSD ResNet-50). Shape and texture carry most of the information, and COCO already contains black-and-white photographs (images 1, 9 and 46 of the dataset).
    • Classes defined by colour suffer most. For SSD MobileNet, AP at IoU 0.5 drops by 0.5 for carrot and traffic light, by 0.34 for cup and by 0.27 for broccoli.
    • Blur hurts far more: mAP falls from 0.450 to 0.239, because blur removes the edges and textures every class relies on, and small objects (bottles, balls, a traffic light) vanish first.
    • Remedies: data augmentation with the same changes (random grayscale, blur, colour jitter) during training, or fine-tuning on data from the new distribution.
    Exercise 4 · Lecture 22, slides 31–42

    Precision–recall values and mAP for one image

    Problem statement

    An object detection model was trained to detect horses. Ground-truth boxes A, B, C, D are shown in blue; detections X, Y, Z in yellow. The table gives each detection's confidence and its IoU with each ground-truth box.

    (a) Report the precision–recall values that you would use to compute mAP at IoU = 0.7 for this single image. Show your work.

    (b) How would mAP change if the IoU threshold were 0.9? Describe the result qualitatively.

    Prerequisite 4.1 · The matching rule

    Process detections from the highest confidence down. A detection is a TP if its best IoU with a still-unmatched ground-truth box reaches the threshold; that box is then used up. Recall always divides by the total number of ground-truth boxes, here 4.

    Warm-up exercise · the lecture's dog example (slides 33–39)

    Five dog detections sorted by score, 3 ground-truth dogs. The outcomes are TP, TP, FP, FP, TP.

    1. Precision and recall after the fourth detection
    2. Precision and recall after the fifth
    Show solution

    After four: \(P = 2/4 = 0.5\), \(R = 2/3\). After five: \(P = 3/5 = 0.6\), \(R = 3/3 = 1\). These are the last two points of slides 37–38.

    Bridge to the question. The horse image is the same procedure with three detections and four objects, but the IoU threshold is 0.7 instead of 0.5.

    LiveChange the IoU threshold and watch the matching
    recall · precision; shaded: AP
    Official solution, step by step
    1. Step 1 · Sort the detections by confidence

      Z (0.93), then Y (0.90), then X (0.85).

      Cheat note

      Highest score first, whatever the IoUs.

    2. Step 2 · Z matches D

      Z's best IoU is 0.79 with D, and \(0.79 \ge 0.7\): a true positive. D is used up.

      $$P = \tfrac{1}{1} = 1, \qquad R = \tfrac{1}{4} .$$
      Cheat note

      Z's IoU with C is only 0.36, so C stays unmatched.

    3. Step 3 · Y matches B

      Y's best IoU is 0.82 with B: a true positive.

      $$P = \tfrac{2}{2} = 1, \qquad R = \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2} .$$
      Cheat note
      $$0.82 \ge 0.7$$
    4. Step 4 · X is a false positive

      X's best IoU is 0.51 with A, below 0.7: no match.

      $$P = \tfrac{2}{3}, \qquad R = \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2} .$$
      DetectionOutcome\(P\)\(R\)
      ZTP (D)11/4
      YTP (B)11/2
      XFP2/31/2
      Cheat note

      X would be a TP at threshold 0.5: the threshold decides.

    5. Step 5 · The resulting AP

      Precision is 1 up to recall \(1/2\), and recall never goes higher; A and C are never found. With one class, mAP equals AP:

      $$\text{AP} = 1 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 0.5 .$$
      Cheat note

      Missed objects cap recall, and the curve has no area beyond it.

    6. Step 6 · (b) IoU threshold 0.9

      No IoU in the table reaches 0.9 (the largest is 0.82), so every detection is a false positive. Precision and recall are 0 throughout, and mAP drops from 0.5 to 0.

      Qualitatively: a stricter threshold demands tighter boxes, so mAP can only stay the same or fall.

      Cheat note
      $$\max \text{IoU} = 0.82 < 0.9$$
    Reference material

    Cheat notes for the four exercises

    One card per exercise: what to remember, the formulas, the answers to the quick checks and warm-ups, and the numbers worth quoting.

    E1Comparing detectors

    Remember
    • Two-stage (Faster R-CNN): RPN proposals, then a per-RoI head. Two looks per object; pays off with strong backbones.
    • One-stage (SSD, RetinaNet, YOLO): classify anchors or grid cells in one pass. Faster.
    • CenterNet: class heatmaps, a peak per object centre, no anchors.
    • Backbone = shared feature extractor; MobileNet is light, ResNet-50 is more accurate.
    Warm-up answers

    Faster R-CNN Inc-ResNet vs SSD R50 time4.5×\(206 / 46\)

    On the 25 images: SSD MobileNet V1 FPN mAP 0.450; SSD ResNet50 V1 FPN mAP 0.521; Faster R-CNN ResNet50 V1 mAP 0.423; CenterNet ResNet50 V1 FPN mAP 0.452.

    E2The score threshold

    Remember
    • A threshold picks one operating point on the P–R curve.
    • Higher threshold: precision up (usually), recall down (always non-increasing).
    • mAP integrates the whole curve, so filtering first can only lower it.
    Formulas
    $$P = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}, \quad R = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}, \quad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R}$$

    E3Modified inputs

    Remember
    • A modified image is a distribution shift from COCO's colour photos.
    • Grayscale keeps shape and texture; blur removes edges and small objects.
    • Remedy: augment training data with the same changes.

    Remember

    Changes to the notebook code

    Small edits so the code runs on current Colab and its outputs are consistent; all outputs shown on this page come from running the edited code.

    1. Cell 27 installs the Object Detection API with pip install .; current pip rejects the old --use-feature=2020-resolver flag.
    2. Cell 23 prints session.url as it is: it already ends in ?polling=true.
    3. Cell 30 converts every image to RGB before inference, and has a GRAYSCALE switch for Exercise 3, which the exercise refers to.
    4. Cell 35 passes eval_key="eval", so the per-sample fields described in section 3(5) are actually written.
    5. Cell 37 keeps the 10 most common classes, as its comment says.
    6. Cell 9's text names the model the code uses, SSD MobileNet V1 FPN 640×640.

    Our run uses TensorFlow 2.21 on a CPU. It reproduces the notebook's saved per-class report exactly except for "book" and "clock", for which the saved run recorded no detections; without those two classes our mAP is the notebook's 0.4292, and with them it is 0.4498.
